## 【206†In std::boxed】

# Struct Box [Button: Copy item path]

1.0.0 · 【207†Source】

    `pub struct Box<T, A = 【208†Global】>(/* private fields */)
    where
        A: 【209†Allocator】,
        T: ?【210†Sized】;`

Expand description

A pointer type that uniquely owns a heap allocation of type `T`.

See the 【206†module-level documentation】 for more.

## Implementations【3†§】

【211†Source】【212†§】

### impl<A> 【213†Box】<dyn 【214†Any】, A>

where A: 【209†Allocator】,

1.0.0 · 【215†Source】
#### pub fn 【52†downcast】<T>(self) -> 【216†Result】<【213†Box】<T, A>, 【213†Box】<dyn 【214†Any】, A>>

where T: 【214†Any】,

Attempts to downcast the box to a concrete type.
##### 【217†§】Examples

    `use std::any::Any;

    fn print_if_string(value: Box<dyn Any>) {
        if let Ok(string) = value.downcast::<String>() {
            println!("String ({}): {}", string.len(), string);
        }
    }

    let my_string = "Hello World".to_string();
    print_if_string(Box::new(my_string));
    print_if_string(Box::new(0i8));`

【218†Source】
#### pub unsafe fn 【55†downcast_unchecked】<T>(self) -> 【213†Box】<T, A>

where T: 【214†Any】,

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`downcast_unchecked` 【219†#90850†github.com】)

Downcasts the box to a concrete type.

For a safe alternative see 【52†`downcast`】.

##### 【220†§】Examples

    `#![feature(downcast_unchecked)]

    use std::any::Any;

    let x: Box<dyn Any> = Box::new(1_usize);

    unsafe {
        assert_eq!(*x.downcast_unchecked::<usize>(), 1);
    }`
##### 【221†§】Safety

The contained value must be of type `T`. Calling this method with the incorrect type is undefined behavior.

### impl<T> 【213†Box】<T>

1.0.0 · 【240†Source】

#### pub fn 【4†new】(x: T) -> 【213†Box】<T>

Allocates memory on the heap and then places `x` into it.

This doesn’t actually allocate if `T` is zero-sized.

##### 【241†§】Examples

    `let five = Box::new(5);`

1.82.0 (const: 【242†unstable†github.com】) · 【243†Source】
#### pub fn 【5†new_uninit】() -> 【213†Box】<【244†MaybeUninit】<T>>

Constructs a new box with uninitialized contents.

##### 【245†§】Examples

    `let mut five = Box::<u32>::new_uninit();
    // Deferred initialization:
    five.write(5);
    let five = unsafe { five.assume_init() };

    assert_eq!(*five, 5)`

1.92.0 · 【246†Source】
#### pub fn 【6†new_zeroed】() -> 【213†Box】<【244†MaybeUninit】<T>>

Constructs a new `Box` with uninitialized contents, with the memory being filled with `0` bytes.

See 【247†`MaybeUninit::zeroed`】 for examples of correct and incorrect usage of this method.

##### 【248†§】Examples

    `let zero = Box::<u32>::new_zeroed();
    let zero = unsafe { zero.assume_init() };

    assert_eq!(*zero, 0)`

1.33.0 · 【249†Source】
#### pub fn 【7†pin】(x: T) -> 【250†Pin】<【213†Box】<T>>

Constructs a new `Pin<Box<T>>`. If `T` does not implement 【251†`Unpin`】, then `x` will be pinned in memory and unable to be moved.

Constructing and pinning of the `Box` can also be done in two steps: `Box::pin(x)` does the same as `【49†Box::into_pin】(【4†Box::new】(x))`. Consider using 【49†`into_pin`】 if you already have a `Box<T>`, or if you want to construct a (pinned) `Box` in a different way than with 【4†`Box::new`】.

【252†Source】
#### pub fn 【8†try_new】(x: T) -> 【216†Result】<【213†Box】<T>, 【253†AllocError】>

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`allocator_api` 【254†#32838†github.com】)

Allocates memory on the heap then places `x` into it, returning an error if the allocation fails

This doesn’t actually allocate if `T` is zero-sized.

##### 【255†§】Examples

    `#![feature(allocator_api)]

    let five = Box::try_new(5)?;`

【256†Source】
#### pub fn 【9†try_new_uninit】() -> 【216†Result】<【213†Box】<【244†MaybeUninit】<T>>, 【253†AllocError】>

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`allocator_api` 【254†#32838†github.com】)

Constructs a new box with uninitialized contents on the heap, returning an error if the allocation fails
##### 【257†§】Examples

    `#![feature(allocator_api)]

    let mut five = Box::<u32>::try_new_uninit()?;
    // Deferred initialization:
    five.write(5);
    let five = unsafe { five.assume_init() };

    assert_eq!(*five, 5);`

【258†Source】
#### pub fn 【10†try_new_zeroed】() -> 【216†Result】<【213†Box】<【244†MaybeUninit】<T>>, 【253†AllocError】>

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`allocator_api` 【254†#32838†github.com】)

Constructs a new `Box` with uninitialized contents, with the memory being filled with `0` bytes on the heap

See 【247†`MaybeUninit::zeroed`】 for examples of correct and incorrect usage of this method.
##### 【259†§】Examples

    `#![feature(allocator_api)]

    let zero = Box::<u32>::try_new_zeroed()?;
    let zero = unsafe { zero.assume_init() };

    assert_eq!(*zero, 0);`

【260†Source】
#### pub fn 【11†map】<U>(this: 【213†Box】<T>, f: impl 【261†FnOnce】(T) -> U) -> 【213†Box】<U>

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`smart_pointer_try_map` 【262†#144419†github.com】)

Maps the value in a box, reusing the allocation if possible.

`f` is called on the value in the box, and the result is returned, also boxed.
Note: this is an associated function, which means that you have to call it as `Box::map(b, f)` instead of `b.map(f)`. This is so that there is no conflict with a method on the inner type.
##### 【263†§】Examples

    `#![feature(smart_pointer_try_map)]

    let b = Box::new(7);
    let new = Box::map(b, |i| i + 7);
    assert_eq!(*new, 14);`

【264†Source】
#### pub fn 【12†try_map】<R>( this: 【213†Box】<T>, f: impl 【261†FnOnce】(T) -> R, ) -> <<R as 【265†Try】>::【266†Residual】 as 【267†Residual】<【213†Box】<<R as 【265†Try】>::【268†Output】>>>::【269†TryType】

where R: 【265†Try】, <R as 【265†Try】>::【266†Residual】: 【267†Residual】<【213†Box】<<R as 【265†Try】>::【268†Output】>>,

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`smart_pointer_try_map` 【262†#144419†github.com】)

Attempts to map the value in a box, reusing the allocation if possible.
`f` is called on the value in the box, and if the operation succeeds, the result is returned, also boxed.

Note: this is an associated function, which means that you have to call it as `Box::try_map(b, f)` instead of `b.try_map(f)`. This is so that there is no conflict with a method on the inner type.
##### 【270†§】Examples

    `#![feature(smart_pointer_try_map)]

    let b = Box::new(7);
    let new = Box::try_map(b, u32::try_from).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(*new, 7);`

【271†Source】【272†§】

### impl<T, A> 【213†Box】<T, A>

#### pub fn 【13†new_in】(x: T, alloc: A) -> 【213†Box】<T, A>

where A: 【209†Allocator】,

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`allocator_api` 【254†#32838†github.com】)

Allocates memory in the given allocator then places `x` into it.

This doesn’t actually allocate if `T` is zero-sized.

##### 【274†§】Examples

    `#![feature(allocator_api)]

    use std::alloc::System;

    let five = Box::new_in(5, System);`

【275†Source】

where A: 【209†Allocator】,

This doesn’t actually allocate if `T` is zero-sized.
##### 【276†§】Examples

    `#![feature(allocator_api)]

【277†Source】

#### pub fn 【15†new_uninit_in】(alloc: A) -> 【213†Box】<【244†MaybeUninit】<T>, A>

where A: 【209†Allocator】,

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`allocator_api` 【254†#32838†github.com】)

Constructs a new box with uninitialized contents in the provided allocator.
##### 【278†§】Examples

    `#![feature(allocator_api)]

    use std::alloc::System;

    let mut five = Box::<u32, _>::new_uninit_in(System);
    // Deferred initialization:
    five.write(5);
    let five = unsafe { five.assume_init() };

    assert_eq!(*five, 5)`

【279†Source】
#### pub fn 【16†try_new_uninit_in】(alloc: A) -> 【216†Result】<【213†Box】<【244†MaybeUninit】<T>, A>, 【253†AllocError】>

【281†Source】
#### pub fn 【17†new_zeroed_in】(alloc: A) -> 【213†Box】<【244†MaybeUninit】<T>, A>

where A: 【209†Allocator】,

🔬This is a nightly-only experimental API. (`allocator_api` 【254†#32838†github.com】)

Constructs a new `Box` with uninitialized contents, with the memory being filled with `0` bytes in the provided allocator.

See 【247†`MaybeUninit::zeroed`】 for examples of correct and incorrect usage of this method.
##### 【282†§】Examples

    `#![feature(allocator_api)]

    use std::alloc::System;

    let zero = Box::<u32, _>::new_zeroed_in(System);
    let zero = unsafe { zero.assume_init() };

    assert_eq!(*zero, 0)`
